title: switch
description: Choosing one of many fixed values, the break you must not forget, and what a switch cannot match.

content.text: Press 3 and the lift goes straight to floor 3. A `switch` takes one value and jumps straight to the matching case, instead of asking `day == 1`, `day == 2`... one by one.

items.sub: The catch-all, like the final `else` in a chain.

steps.note: Look at `day` once: it is 3. Jump to the matching case.
Here is `case 3:`. Cases 1 and 2 were never run.

content.title: Jump to the match
content.outro: `day` is written once, not on every line like an `else if` chain, so it cannot be mistyped halfway down.

content.value: The break You Must Not Forget

items.title: With break
No break
items.text: Day 1 prints Monday, then keeps going into case 2.

content.title: With and without break
content.caption: Write `break` on the last case too: the day you add another case below it, it is already correct.

steps.note: ...so C++ falls into case 2 and runs that too.

content.title: Fall-through
content.outro: This is called **fall-through**: running on into the next case. It compiles fine, so the output is your only clue.

content.question: No `break` anywhere, `day = 2`. What prints?
content.explain: C++ jumps to `case 2`, then falls through every case below it, including `default`.

content.caption: Fall-through on purpose: stacked cases with no code between them share one block. Days 6 and 7 both reach `Weekend!`.

content.value: A switch also works on a `char`, which suits menus. A `char` case uses single quotes, like `case 'a':`.

steps.note: `'q'` is not `'Q'`: matching is exact. No match here.

content.title: A menu with a char switch
content.outro: Stacking `case 'q':` and `case 'Q':` lets both letters quit.

content.value: A switch only matches whole numbers and `char` values. `switch (command)` on a `string` is a compile error. Use an `else if` chain with `==` instead.

content.caption: The fix for text: compare with `==` and finish with an `else` as the catch-all.

content.title: A new variable inside a case
content.caption: Braces give the variable its own block, so the other cases are safely outside it.

content.question: Which of these can follow the word `case`?
content.explain: A case must be a fixed whole number or `char`. Text, comparisons and variables are not allowed.

content.value: Both tools pick one path out of many. The deciding question is: fixed values, or ranges?

items.title: switch
items.text: One whole number or `char` against **fixed** values: menu options, day numbers, grade letters.

content.title: switch or else if?
content.caption: A switch never does anything a chain cannot. For the right shape it is shorter and clearer: just remember every `break`.

content.question: Which tool fits "temperature above 30 is hot, above 20 is warm"?
content.explain: These are ranges. A switch can only match fixed values, so use an `else if` chain.

quiz.question: What does `break` do inside a switch?
options: Ends the switch, so C++ does not run the cases below
quiz.explain: Without it, C++ falls through into the next case and keeps going until it finds a `break` or reaches the end.

quiz.question: A switch on `day` matches `case 1`, which has no `break`. What happens?
options: The cases below it also run, until a break is found
The program stops with an error
quiz.explain: This is fall-through. It compiles cleanly, so the wrong output is the only sign that a `break` is missing.

quiz.question: What is `default` in a switch?
options: The catch-all, like the final `else` in a chain
The case that always runs first
A required label on every case
quiz.explain: `default` runs when no case matched. Leaving it out means an unexpected value does nothing at all.

quiz.question: Which of these can a switch NOT do?
quiz.explain: A switch compares against fixed known values only. Ranges and comparisons need an `else if` chain.

quiz.question: Can you write `switch (command)` when `command` is a `string`?
options: Yes, as long as every case is in double quotes.
Yes, but only with a default case.
No: it is a compile error, so use an `else if` chain with `==`.
quiz.explain: A C++ switch needs a whole number or a `char`. For text, compare with `==` in a chain.

quiz.question: A case declares `int bonus = 10;` and the compiler says `jump to case label`. What fixes it?
options: Wrap that case's instructions in their own braces
Move the default case to the top
quiz.explain: The braces give the variable its own small block, so no other case can jump past its setup.
